mappings.note: The work is converting a measured map distance into ground distance using a stated scale, which is the scale half of LO-4; LO-3 is cited because the two points are river estuaries on the map of India. Not LO-2, since no latitude or longitude is read.

Answered by reading India's standard meridian (82.5 E) against Greenwich, so it is longitude identification (LO-2); C-SST1.1-LO-3 is added because the 15-degrees-per-hour rule comes from the rotation that makes day and night. Not LO-4, no scale or symbol is involved.
Purely about conventional symbols and colours as map furniture, which LO-4 names explicitly. Not LO-1: no direction is being located.

Asks the pupil to orient themselves and name what lies in each of the eight directions, i.e. locating directions on a flat surface. LO-4 is the near sibling but nothing is drawn to scale with symbols here.

Distinguishing local from standard time turns on which meridian you reckon by (LO-2) and on the sun's apparent motion from rotation (C-SST1.1-LO-3). Not LO-1, which is about compass directions, not time.

The whole point is that local time follows longitude and not latitude - a discrimination inside LO-2. C-SST1.1-LO-3 is not cited because no rotation arithmetic is needed: the answer is zero difference.
A true/false on the Equator's status among the parallels, which is latitude identification. Not the competency, since the specific outcome fits.
The International Date Line is a meridian (LO-2) and the thing it changes is the day and date (C-SST1.1-LO-3). Not LO-4: it is not a conventional map symbol.
Tests knowing that a map is the tool for finding places in an unfamiliar city. Held at competency level because no outcome covers choosing or using a map as an artefact - LO-4 is about drawing one.
Definition of a map as a view from above. Competency level for the same reason: LO-4 asks for a map to be drawn, which this does not.
Definition of an atlas. No outcome mentions atlases; LO-1 concerns continents and oceans, which this does not ask for.
Asks which TYPE of map shows countries, states and capitals - a question about kinds of maps, which no outcome enumerates. Not LO-2, since no latitude or longitude is read off.
Identifies scale as the component that lets a large area fit a small sheet; scale is named in LO-4. Not the competency, because the specific outcome does cover scale.
A direct scale computation (3 cm at 1 cm = 500 m). Same outcome as the other scale items because LO-4 is the only one naming scale; the questions differ in task but share the one fitting outcome.
Asks why scale must be known before measuring - the reasoning behind the same LO-4 scale element, rather than an arithmetic application of it.
Names the four cardinal directions, which is exactly locating directions on a flat surface. Not LO-4, which needs scale and symbols alongside direction.
Intermediate directions (NE, SW) extend the same direction-locating outcome one step finer than the cardinal-points item.
The N arrow is the device that fixes direction on a flat map, so LO-1. Not LO-4, because the north arrow is an orientation aid rather than a feature symbol.
Identifies the Survey of India as the standardiser of conventional symbols - the symbol clause of LO-4. Not LO-3, which is about physical features, not who codifies their signs.
Matches a feature to its conventional symbol, the core of LO-4's symbol clause. Not LO-3: a road and a railway are not India's physical features.

Earth's near-spherical shape as the reason flat maps are hard - a map-projection point with no matching outcome. Not C-SST1.1-LO-2, which concerns the earth as a habitat and its spheres, not its geometry.
The orange-peel demonstration of why a sphere cannot be flattened; projection distortion is covered by the competency but by none of its outcomes.
Globe versus flat map for accuracy. Held at competency level: LO-2 mentions the globe only as the surface on which latitudes are identified, which is not what is asked.
Requires reading a direction (south) off a printed town map to find a feature - locating directions on a flat surface. Not LO-4, since the pupil reads a given map rather than drawing one.
The chessboard pair-of-coordinates analogy is the textbook's lead-in to the latitude/longitude grid, so LO-2. Not the competency, because the grid idea is precisely what LO-2 names.
Identifies the poles, which LO-2 lists by name. Not C-SST1.1-LO-3: the question asks what the fixed points are called, not what the rotation produces.
Definition of the Equator, named explicitly in LO-2. Distinct in task from the item on the Equator's size, but the frame offers only this one outcome for both.
Defines latitude as angular distance north or south of the Equator - the latitude half of LO-2. Not LO-4, no map drawing involved.
Which parallel is the largest circle; a property of the parallels system inside LO-2 rather than of any single named line.
The Equator's 0-degree value - the numbering convention of the latitude grid, squarely LO-2.
Pole latitudes of 90 N and 90 S; LO-2 names the poles as things to be identified on a globe. Not the goal-level code, since the outcome fits exactly.

Names the torrid zone by its position relative to the Equator, so it is read off the latitude framework of LO-2. Not C-SST1.1-LO-2, whose zones are the spheres of the earth including the biosphere, not heat belts.
Unlike the zone-naming items, this asks WHY climate moderates poleward, whose answer is the changing angle of sunlight - hence C-SST1.1-LO-3 alongside the latitude outcome.
Names the frigid zone from its polar latitude - the mirror of the torrid-zone item and mapped the same way, since the frame offers one latitude outcome for both.
Defines meridians of longitude, the longitude half of LO-2. Not C-SST1.1-LO-3 - the poles appear only as the meridians' endpoints, not as an axis of rotation.
The 0-to-180 range of longitude east and west of the Prime Meridian; the numbering convention of the longitude grid in LO-2.
That a latitude and a longitude together fix a place is the synthesis LO-2 is built on. Not the competency, which would lose that specificity.
India's latitudinal extent, 8 N to 37 N - LO-2 explicitly covers identifying latitudes for India on the world map. Not LO-3, which is about India's physical features rather than its grid position.
India's longitudinal extent, 68 E to 97 E; the longitude counterpart of the latitudinal-extent item, and again LO-2 rather than LO-3.
Converts 30 E into a local time from Greenwich noon: longitude identification (LO-2) plus the rotation rule behind day and night (C-SST1.1-LO-3). Not LO-4, nothing to do with scale or symbols.
